source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.2, printed page 8: ionic radius and its trends (Figure 1.5; the printed radii in picometres are not reproduced).

blocks.text: The ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion in a crystal lattice, defined as the distance from the nucleus of an ion to its outermost electron shell, in picometres or angstroms. When an atom loses one or more electrons to become a positive ion it generally becomes smaller than the neutral atom, because the loss of electrons reduces electronic repulsion and lets the remaining electrons be pulled closer to the nucleus. When an atom gains one or more electrons to become an anion it generally becomes larger than the neutral atom, because the added electrons increase electronic repulsion, the nuclear pull on each electron decreases and the electron cloud expands.

blocks.alt: A grid of atoms and their ions drawn to scale, with radii in picometres. Left: lithium, beryllium, sodium, magnesium, aluminium, potassium, calcium, gallium, rubidium, strontium and indium, each with a grey atom beside a smaller red cation (for example Na 186, Na+ 95). Right: nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, sulfur, chlorine, selenium, bromine, tellurium and iodine, each with a grey atom beside a larger blue anion (for example Cl 99, Cl- 181).
blocks.caption: Variation in ionic radius (ions in red and blue, parent atoms brown; radii in picometres) (original diagram after Figure 1.5).

blocks.text: Across a period from left to right the ionic radius of cations decreases, because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer; the radius of anions also decreases across a period for the same reason. Down a group both cations and anions increase in size, because the principal quantum number n increases, more electron shells are added, and the greater distance of the outermost electrons from the nucleus outweighs the effect of the increased nuclear charge.
